L23: TLDR
L24:   1. Document: Class Action Complaint, Buist et al. v. Anthropic PBC, OpenAI OpCo LLC, SpaceXAI LLC, and Google LLC, N.D. Cal.
L25:   2. San Francisco Division, Case No. 3:26-cv-10693, Document 1, filed 18 September 2026 (29 pages).
L26:   3. Cause: Sherman Act Section 1, with Clayton Sections 4 and 16 remedies, on a theory that a public pacing essay plus CEO assent formed a horizontal agreement to slow capability improvement.
L27:   4. Class: U.S. direct paid subscribers to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini from 12 September 2026 onward.
L28:   5. Prayer: class certification, liability finding, treble damages, an injunction against horizontal pacing restraints, and fees.
L29:   6. This Record excerpts the filing; it does not adjudicate it.
L30: ## Document
L31: 
L32:   * Title: Class Action Complaint

L38:   * Primary URL: cite19†RECAP PDF†storage.courtlistener.com L39: ## Parties
L40: 
L41: Plaintiffs (named): Charles Buist (FL); Cheyenne Hunt (CA); Christine Bullock (CA); Nick Spetsas (FL). Each alleges paid consumer subscriptions during the class period.
L42: 
L43: Defendants: Anthropic, PBC; OpenAI OpCo, LLC; SpaceXAI LLC; Google LLC.
L44: 
L45: Counsel (as captioned): Trial Lawyers for Justice (Rowley, Tutt, Jones, Norman).
L46: ## Claim excerpted
L47: 
L48: Single claim for relief: Violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1, against all defendants (¶¶135-147 area).
L49: Core allegation (paraphrase of ¶¶1, 137-140): beginning no later than 12 September 2026 (and on information and belief earlier), defendants entered a contract, combination, or conspiracy to restrain the pace at which they develop and improve competing frontier-AI products.
L50: Manifestation pleaded through Amodei's We Must Pace the Frontier proposal; Musk, Altman, and Hassabis public assent on 12 September; Anthropic-OpenAI-Google working-group meetings since July; Altman's 14 September "slower than it otherwise could be" statement; and policy-chief confirmation of collaboration.
L51: Legal characterizations pleaded in the alternative: naked horizontal restraint unlawful per se; quick-look; rule of reason.
L52: ## Class excerpted
L53: 
L54: Nationwide Class (¶123): All persons in the United States who, from 12 September 2026 through the date effects cease, purchased directly from one or more Defendants a paid individual consumer subscription providing premium access to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini.
L55: 
L56: Subclass mirrors per defendant. Plaintiffs reserve moving the start date earlier after discovery.
L57: ## Relief excerpted
L58: 
L59: Prayer (WHEREFORE):
L60: 
L61:   * Class certification and appointment of class counsel
L62:   * Decree of Section 1 violation
L63:   * Damages trebled under Clayton Act § 4
L64:   * Preliminary and permanent injunction under Clayton Act § 16 against continuing/renewing/enforcing/implementing horizontal agreements to restrain competitive innovation
L65:   * Interest, attorneys' fees, costs, further relief
L66: Injunction targets listed at ¶150 include agreed limits on development rate, compute/training runs under a pacing arrangement, agreed limits on AI-developing-AI, coordinated release delays, capability checkpoints used as horizontal restraints, and information exchange to police such restraints. ¶151 preserves unilateral safety measures, independent slowing, independent evaluators, petitioning government, and non-collusive standard-setting.

L99@P1: CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
L100@P1: INTRODUCTION
L101@P1: 1. This action challenges an agreement among the four companies at the frontier of artificial intelligence—Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google—to slow the pace at which each
L102@P1: company improves the competing products it sells to consumers.
L103@P1: 2. The agreement was proposed in public, accepted in public, and confirmed in public. On
L104@P1: the morning of September 12, 2026, Anthropic’s Chief Executive Officer, Dario Amodei, published an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier. It declared: “We must slow the pace at which we
L105@P1: improve the capabilities of AI models.” It called for “industry-wide coordination” among frontier
L106@P1: laboratories to set “limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress,” and it explained that coordinated
L107@P1: slowing would let each participant reduce its pace “without sacrificing commercial advantage.”
L108@P1: 3. Amodei’s rivals confirmed their agreement the same day. Within about an hour, Elon
L109@P1: Musk, who founded and controls SpaceXAI’s Grok business, quote-posted the proposal and wrote:
L110@P1: “Dario is right.” OpenAI’s Chief Executive Officer, Sam Altman, wrote: “I agree with Dario that
L111@P1: we need to pace the frontier,” and committed OpenAI to the first concrete step of Amodei’s plan.
L112@P1: Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis called the essay “the right path forward” and tied
L113@P1: it to the “industry-wide standards body for frontier AI” he had proposed two months earlier as a
L114@P1: vehicle through which the laboratories could coordinate.
L115@P1: 4. Two days later, Altman said what pacing meant: AI progress “should be slower than it
L116@P1: otherwise could be.” He added that OpenAI would not wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation
L117@P1: before beginning that work with its “colleagues across the industry.” The following day, OpenAI’s
L118@P1: Global Policy Chief confirmed that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had already been
L119@P1: working together for weeks, reportedly through a working group of company representatives that
L120@P1: had met regularly since July.
L121@P1: 5. Defendants themselves have explained why they needed an agreement. Frontier-AI companies compete above all by improving their models faster than their rivals: better reasoning, better
L122@P1: coding, more capable agents, larger context windows, new features. A July 2026 statement signed
L123@P1: by Amodei, OpenAI’s Chief Scientist, a Google DeepMind co-founder, and dozens of their

L153@P2: CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
L154@P2: colleagues acknowledged that each company faces “intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow” development. A firm that slows alone loses customers, revenue, and technological leadership to rivals that keep going. Amodei’s proposal solved that problem the way cartels always
L155@P2: have: by agreeing to slow together, so that no participant bears the competitive cost of restraint.
L156@P2: 6. An agreement among competitors to reduce the quality of their products and the rate at
L157@P2: which those products improve is an agreement to restrict output. It is among the restraints Section
L158@P2: 1 of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1, has always condemned, and it does not become lawful because the products are new.
L159@P2: 7. Plaintiffs take AI safety seriously. Plaintiffs, and each of them, believe that AI should
L160@P2: have guardrails with ethical considerations and direct liability for any breach being paramount.
L161@P2: Those guardrails and consequences should not be decided by the Defendants, but by we the people,
L162@P2: through state and federal regulation, and through the voices of juries in our communities.
L163@P2: 8. Artificial intelligence is among the most consequential technologies in human history.
L164@P2: Researchers have used it to predict the three-dimensional structure of nearly every protein known
L165@P2: to science, to identify cancers from imaging studies with accuracy matching or exceeding trained
L166@P2: specialists, to accelerate the development of new materials for clean energy, to solve previously
L167@P2: unsolved mathematical problems, and to compress years of scientific labor into days. It is undisputed that AI alone could add trillions of dollars annually to the global economy. These are not
L168@P2: hypothetical gains. They are the product of the competitive race that Defendants’ agreement now
L169@P2: threatens to slow.
L170@P2: 9. Plaintiffs recognize that powerful technology carries real risks, and they take those risks
L171@P2: seriously. But the lesson of every previous transformative industry is that safety and responsibility
L172@P2: are properly the work of each company acting on its own, not a cartel license. Automobile manufacturers do not allow ordinary passenger vehicles to accelerate to 300 miles per hour. They do not
L173@P2: need a horizontal agreement among the major car manufacturers to make that choice: engineering
L174@P2: constraints, internal safety standards, product-liability exposure, government regulation through
L175@P2: the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, and basic competitive self-interest each

L205@P3: CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
L206@P3: independently supply the guardrail. The same logic applies here. Each Defendant is free, and indeed obligated, to set its own safety thresholds, retain its own evaluators, build its own product
L207@P3: guardrails, and restrain its own development. None of that requires an agreement with rivals.
L208@P3: 10. Defendants are also well-positioned to lead on environmental responsibility, and to do
L209@P3: so on their own. AI’s energy footprint is substantial and growing: training a single large frontier
L210@P3: model can consume tens of millions of kilowatt-hours of electricity, and the International Energy
L211@P3: Agency projects that, by 2030, global data-center electricity demand will more than double from
L212@P3: 2024 levels, driven in significant part by AI workloads. Each Defendant has pledged environmental commitments. Each has the engineers, the capital, and the competitive incentive to pursue more
L213@P3: efficient training architectures, cleaner energy procurement, and smarter compute scheduling. Innovation in AI efficiency—models that do more with less energy—is itself a domain of competitive advantage. An agreement to slow capability development does nothing to make AI more environmentally sound; only engineering competition, applied to efficiency as a prize, will.
L214@P3: 11. In short, the path to responsible, safe, and environmentally conscious AI development
L215@P3: is each company doing the right thing: investing in safety research, adopting rigorous internal
L216@P3: evaluations, reducing its environmental footprint, and welcoming government oversight and regulation. That path is fully open to every Defendant. What the antitrust laws forbid is the shortcut
L217@P3: of competitors agreeing among themselves to substitute collective restraint for individual accountability. This action is brought in defense of the competitive process that makes genuine responsibility and genuine progress possible.
L218@P3: 12. The antitrust laws do not permit competitors to decide among themselves that competition is too dangerous. Whether frontier AI should develop more slowly is a question for each
L219@P3: company acting alone, or for Congress and the agencies. It is not a question that four competitors
L220@P3: may answer together. The law leaves each Defendant free to be as cautious, as responsible, and as
L221@P3: environmentally conscious as it chooses to be, just not through agreement with the companies it
L222@P3: competes against.

L252@P4: CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
L253@P4: 13. Plaintiffs support each Defendant’s responsibility to consider its conduct carefully and
L254@P4: do not challenge any Defendant’s unilateral decisions about safety, testing, environmental impacts,
L255@P4: or the pace of its own development. Each Defendant remains free to slow itself, to retain outside
L256@P4: evaluators, to adopt its own product guardrails, to reduce its environmental impacts, and to ask
L257@P4: Congress for regulation or an antitrust exemption. Plaintiffs challenge only what the antitrust laws
L258@P4: forbid: an agreement among competitors about how fast their competing products will improve.
L259@P4: Congress has granted no exemption for that agreement. Amodei wrote that the government would
L260@P4: need to issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations; Altman announced that
L261@P4: OpenAI would proceed without it.
L262@P4: 14. Plaintiffs are consumers who pay a Defendant directly for subscriptions to one or more
L263@P4: of the following services—ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini. The value of those subscriptions
L264@P4: consists of access to Defendants’ most capable models and to the improvements Defendants continually release. Defendants market and price those subscriptions on exactly that basis. An agreement that slows improvement lowers the quality of what subscribers receive for the price they pay.
L265@P4: That is an overcharge, and it is an injury of the kind the antitrust laws were enacted to prevent.
L266@P4: 15. Plaintiffs bring this action on behalf of a nationwide class of direct purchasers of paid
L267@P4: consumer subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini for treble damages under Section
L268@P4: 4 of the Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15, and for injunctive relief under Section 16, 15 U.S.C. § 26, to
L269@P4: restore the condition the antitrust laws require: that each Defendant decide for itself, in competition
L270@P4: with the others, how aggressively to develop and improve its products.
L271@P4: PARTIES
L272@P4: A. Plaintiffs
L273@P4: 16. Plaintiff Charles Buist is a resident of Florida. During the Class Period, he personally
L274@P4: purchased a paid individual consumer subscription to Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini. He
L275@P4: continues to subscribe and intends to continue subscribing.
